entries.title: Article: The iOS Crash We Could Not Reproduce
entries.summary: This article describes the investigation to find the root cause of a production crash in a large-scale iOS consumer app that had no clean stack trace. The crash occurred intermittently and resisted every local reproduction attempt. The final code change was small, but identifying the root cause required turning a vague SIGBUS report into a controlled set of experiments. By Abhishek Gang Deb
entries.content:
Key Takeaways

  • Intermittent production crashes often need controlled fault isolation when logs and local testing cannot identify the failing path.
  • A lower overall crash rate does not prove that the root cause is fixed. Unrelated changes can simply change the timing of a concurrency defect.
  • One device that reproduces a failure probabilistically can turn speculative debugging into testable engineering work.
  • HTML import through 
    NSAttributedString
    has a main-thread requirement that is easy to miss when the call sits inside asynchronous screen preparation.
  • A shared main-actor abstraction is a stronger safeguard than asking every call site to remember a framework threading rule.

Some production crashes announce themselves with a clean stack trace. This one did not. It appeared in a large-scale consumer iOS application, affected only some executions, and resisted every local reproduction attempt. The final code change was small, but reaching it required turning a vague 

SIGBUS
report into a controlled set of experiments. This article walks through the investigation and the threading contract behind HTML import in 
NSAttributedString
.

The Crash That Refused to Reproduce

Most production crashes I investigate start with a familiar routine. I read the crash report, look for the stack frame closest to the failure, try to reproduce the path, and then work backward toward the root cause. This incident did not fit that pattern.

The crash showed up in a large-scale consumer iOS application. It affected only a subset of executions and appeared at unpredictable times. Exact production metrics are confidential, but the incident was serious enough to require a focused investigation and an expedited hotfix.

Neither developers nor QA engineers could reproduce it consistently. We could repeat the customer flow without seeing anything unusual. The crash report included a SIGBUS signal and Foundation frames related to attributed string processing, but it did not point to a clear line in our Swift code.

SIGBUS is a low-level invalid memory access signal, not a diagnosis. It can come from several conditions, so it would have been wrong to assume from the signal alone that a specific variable had been released or reused. The evidence narrowed the search area, but it did not establish the cause.

That left a wide search space. I considered object lifetime, SwiftUI view model ownership, shared mutable state, unsynchronized work, and Foundation behavior. Management needed an answer quickly, and I initially had about a week to investigate and prepare a fix.

Starting With the Expected Suspects

I started with the checks that usually help with this kind of failure. I enabled Zombie Objects, added exception and symbolic breakpoints, reviewed ownership around the affected screens, and inspected the asynchronous paths that prepared their data.

I also made defensive improvements while I was in that part of the codebase. I tightened observable object ownership, reviewed whether several reference types really needed identity semantics, clarified synchronization, and made UI-related concurrency more explicit with async and await and MainActor isolation.

Those changes improved the code. The first hotfix also produced a noticeable reduction in the overall crash rate. But the original crash signature continued to appear in production, and customers were still reporting the behavior tied to the incident.

Why the First Hotfix Misled Us

The initial improvement looked encouraging because the aggregate crash rate moved in the right direction. It did not prove causation. Changes to lifecycle handling and synchronization can affect task scheduling, object retention, and timing. A timing-sensitive failure can become less frequent even when the underlying contract violation is still present.

That distinction became central to the investigation. We had improved the application, but we had not shown that we had removed the defect. The target crash still existed, and the remaining investigation window had narrowed to only a few days.

A Reproducible Device Changed the Investigation

The turning point was not another breakpoint or a more detailed stack trace. A QA engineer who also used the production application found that she could trigger the crash by repeating the affected flow. It was still intermittent and sometimes took four or five attempts, but that was enough.

For the first time, I had a practical test oracle. If a new build still crashed on that device, the change had not addressed the problem. If repeated attempts stopped producing the failure, the change deserved deeper validation. The device changed the work from production forensics into an experiment.

Turning Debugging Into an Experiment

My first experiments still focused on the screens closest to the visible failure. I cleaned up their code, adjusted ownership, reviewed asynchronous work, generated an IPA, and sent it to the QA engineer.

After several attempts, that build crashed again. The result was negative, but it was useful. Until then, I had been making reasonable changes without a reliable way to know whether they mattered. A reproducible failure made every rejected hypothesis informative.

The loop became simple: change one area, build an IPA, install it on the affected device, repeat the customer flow, and record whether the crash returned. Across the investigation, I shared roughly nine or ten experimental builds.

I also explored potential solutions through developer communities, including Stack Overflow, the Apple Developer Forums, and LinkedIn iOS development groups. However, the application's source code and internal debugging artifacts were confidential under company policies, so I could only discuss the problem at a general technical level without sharing proprietary information. While these communities offered opportunities to explore possible causes, they could not directly inspect or conclusively diagnose the issue. I therefore continued investigating through controlled experiments within our development environment.

Systematic Fault Isolation

I changed the question. Instead of asking which code looked suspicious, I asked which code had to remain for the crash to survive. I removed one view or behavior at a time, generated a new build, and tested the same flow on the affected device.

After six or seven elimination builds, the failure surface narrowed to one file. Nothing in that file looked obviously unsafe, so I repeated the process inside it. Several more experiments reduced the problem to one operation.

The line converted HTML data into an attributed string:

let attributedString = try NSMutableAttributedString(
    data: data,
    options: [
        .documentType: NSAttributedString.DocumentType.html
    ],
    documentAttributes: nil
)

The code had no force unwrap, unsafe pointer, manual memory management, or obvious shared state. At the call site, it looked like a normal Foundation conversion. That ordinary appearance had kept it low on the original list of suspects.

The Disclosure Code Path

The affected flow involved two important views of the application. Each view displayed a static disclosure section near the bottom, containing legal and informational text formatted as HTML. Although the content itself was static, it included interactive elements such as hyperlinks and phone numbers that users could tap to open external web views or initiate phone calls.

The application received this disclosure content as HTML and converted it into an attributed string before rendering it on the screen.

Because the disclosure section was relatively small and worked correctly during most executions, it initially appeared unlikely to be responsible for the crash. Attention naturally focused on the larger architectural components and asynchronous screen-loading operations.

The critical issue was that HTML-to-attributed-string conversion could be invoked from an asynchronous screen-preparation path without an explicit guarantee of main-thread execution. This mattered because Foundation's HTML importer has a threading constraint that was not enforced at the call site.

The Hidden Threading Contract

Apple documents an important constraint for HTML import through 

NSAttributedString
: when the options specify HTML as the document type, the importer should not be called from a background thread. Apple says the method may try to synchronize with the main thread, fail, and time out. The broader attributed string documentation also notes that WebKit handles HTML conversion, which matters because this path is not just a pure data transformation.

Our problem was therefore not that the screens displayed attributed text. The unsafe condition came from creating HTML-backed attributed strings from an execution context where the main thread was not guaranteed.

The API did not make that requirement obvious at the call site. It accepted a Data value and returned an attributed string, so it looked like a straightforward transformation. The implementation carried a platform constraint that the surrounding asynchronous architecture had to enforce.

Why the Failure Appeared Random

Timing-dependent defects can survive many successful executions. Two users may receive equivalent HTML and call the same Swift function, yet reach the importer under different scheduling conditions. One execution may occur safely while another reaches the same code from background work during screen preparation.

This also explained why the defensive hotfix reduced the observed frequency without removing the signature. Lifecycle and synchronization changes changed timing. They did not eliminate the unsupported execution context.

The practical lesson was clear: changing the probability of a concurrency failure is not the same as removing its cause. For this incident to be considered resolved, the targeted crash signature and the reproducing flow both had to confirm the fix.

Turning the Fix Into an Application Wide Guarantee

The immediate repair was to perform the HTML conversion on the main actor. Fixing only the original call site would have addressed the visible incident, but it would not have prevented the same mistake elsewhere in a large codebase.

I searched for every place where the application converted HTML into an attributed string. Then I introduced a shared helper that made the execution requirement part of the API instead of an instruction each developer had to remember. The following code is a simplified and anonymized representation of that design:

enum HTMLAttributedStringRenderer {
    @MainActor
    static func render(from data: Data) throws -> NSAttributedString {
        try NSMutableAttributedString(
            data: data,
            options: [
                .documentType: NSAttributedString.DocumentType.html
            ],
            documentAttributes: nil
        )
    }
}

The UI-facing caller also stayed isolated to the main actor:

@MainActor
func updateDisclosure(from data: Data) throws {
    disclosureText = try HTMLAttributedStringRenderer.render(from: data)
}

Existing call sites were routed through this helper. The design centralized the Foundation dependency, reduced duplication, and created one place to document and test the threading contract. More importantly, it turned the requirement from a convention into a code-level boundary.

This did not mean all screen preparation moved to the main actor. Networking, decoding, and other suitable work could remain asynchronous. Only the operation with the framework constraint, along with the UI state that consumed its result, needed explicit main-actor isolation.

Validating the Complete Fix

I sent the corrected build to the QA engineer and asked her to repeat the flow on the device that had exposed every earlier attempt. The failure no longer appeared. I then asked for additional testing across both affected views and nearby behavior before promoting the change to the hotfix branch.

After release, production monitoring showed a dramatic reduction in the targeted crash. Exact figures cannot be disclosed, but this outcome differed from the first hotfix in the way that mattered: the specific production signature no longer appeared at a meaningful rate.

The investigation ended with three validations rather than one. The known device stopped reproducing the issue, every related call site used the shared helper, and production monitoring confirmed the expected change.

What the Incident Changed

The most useful lesson was broader than one Foundation API. When evidence is incomplete, a debugging process has to create new evidence. A device that reproduced the crash intermittently was more valuable than a long list of plausible code changes because it allowed each hypothesis to fail clearly.

The incident also changed how I evaluate framework abstractions. A Swift initializer may look safe while hiding behavior inherited from Objective-C, Foundation, UIKit, WebKit, run loops, or older platform design. Swift concurrency makes execution context easier to express, but it does not automatically make every underlying API safe for concurrent use.

Finally, a successful repair should make the same defect harder to reintroduce. The shared helper mattered because it protected future call sites, not only the two views involved in the incident.

A Practical Investigation Checklist

  • Treat a signal such as SIGBUS as evidence about the failure category, not as proof of one memory-management cause.
  • Track the specific crash signature separately from the overall crash rate so unrelated improvements do not create false confidence.
  • When one device can reproduce the issue intermittently, preserve that environment and use it as a controlled test target.
  • Change or remove one area at a time, and keep a record of which build accepted or rejected each hypothesis.
  • After identifying a framework contract, search the full codebase and enforce the rule through a shared abstraction when possible.
  • Validate the fix through targeted reproduction, regression testing, and post-release production monitoring.

Conclusion

The final code change was small. The hard part was reaching it through incomplete crash information, an unreproducible flow, misleading early improvements, time pressure, and proprietary artifacts that could not be shared outside the organization.

Once a single device reproduced the failure, the investigation stopped depending on intuition. Repeated builds narrowed the problem from two screens to one file and then to one ordinary-looking Foundation call. The root cause was HTML import running without the main-thread guarantee required by its implementation.

When a stack trace cannot identify the bug, the next step is to design an experiment that forces the code to reveal it. In this incident, systematic fault isolation provided the evidence that ordinary debugging could not.

entries.title: Angular's TypeScript 7-Powered Compiler Enters Beta with Rust-Based Preprocessor
entries.summary: The Angular team has introduced ngp, a compiler preprocessor that rewrites the analysis stage in Rust using Oxc. It replaces ngc's dependence on the Transformer API, which TypeScript 7.0 removed. An early benchmark showed 2x to 3x faster cold builds. Adoption is expected in an Angular 22 minor release; production builds should stay on ngc until then. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
The Angular team has shared details of a new version of its compiler, the Angular Preprocessor (ngp), which rewrites the analysis stage of the toolchain in Rust to clear the way for TypeScript 7 adoption. Alex Rickabaugh and Mark Techson announced the work on the Angular team blog in late September, shortly after Microsoft shipped TypeScript 7.0, whose Go-based rewrite removed the 

ts.Transformer
API that Angular's ahead-of-time compiler depends on.

The existing compiler, 

ngc
, wraps 
tsc
and uses the Transformer API to turn decorators such as 
@Component
and 
@Pipe
into runtime instructions. The Go port offers no cross-language equivalent, and crossing the JS/Go boundary at every file would be prohibitive. The Angular team's answer is to decouple compilation from TypeScript's APIs and rebuild it on Oxc, the VoidZero Rust toolchain already powering Vite. The team pointed to the plan on X, framing it as a partial rewrite rather than a fresh start. 

ngp
runs in three stages. A Rust frontend using Oxc analyses files in parallel to discover Angular declarations and resolve metadata. The existing TypeScript template compiler then emits two artefacts, a runtime file containing the transformed component and a 
.ngtypecheck.ts
file holding the Type Check Block (TCB) for template type-checking. Finally a downstream tool, whether 
tsgo
, 
tsrs
, 
esbuild
or Rolldown, handles type-checking and JavaScript emission independently.

The bulk of 

ngp
landed on 8 October in a single commit of more than 370,000 lines, around 56,000 of them Rust. Cédric Exbrayat of Ninja Squad benchmarked the beta against three projects ranging from 15 to 1,714 components and measured a 2x to 3x speedup on cold builds, with memory use on the largest project falling from 2.8 GB to 1.4 GB. Pairing ngp with 
tsrs
and Rolldown gave the fastest pipeline, with 
tsgo
and 
esbuild
only marginally slower. They concluded there is further gains to be made:

This is already very promising, and there are certainly further gains to be made when the team focuses on performance optimization.

Christopher Holder at push-based.io took a different tack, writing 

vite-plugin-ngp
to compile Angular files on demand. On the Super Productivity codebase (252 components), the dev server reached the first page in 10.5 seconds against 17.4 for 
ng serve
, with template edits applying in 112 milliseconds rather than a 2.6 second full reload. On a generated 5,000-component app the gap widened to 1.6 seconds against 28.4. Holder cautioned that the plugin "is a prototype on a prototype" pinned to 
22.3.0-next.2
.

On Reddit, a number of developers are excited about the update and write up, with one commenting:

Read the whole article. Impressive. The Angular team surpassed my expectations!

VoidZero's own experimental Oxc Angular compiler, covered by InfoQ in April, reported a roughly 97% improvement on narrower workloads but is now described as "actively seeking maintainers". The Angular team confirmed VoidZero's work influenced the architecture and that the two groups have been collaborating, with 

ngp
becoming the official path.

Teams on earlier Angular versions should first run the standard update guide to reach v20 or later. Adoption of 

ngp
is expected to land in a minor release of Angular 22 once TypeScript 7.1 restores the compiler API; until then production builds should stay on 
ngc
.

Angular is Google's open-source, TypeScript-first web framework, widely adopted across enterprise applications and built around standalone components and signal-based reactivity.

entries.title: Cloudflare Makes Basin Serverless Analytics Generally Available
entries.summary: Cloudflare has announced the general availability of Basin, a serverless analytics platform built on Apache Iceberg and R2 Object Storage. The managed service supports open data formats and integrates with tools such as DuckDB, Snowflake, and Apache Spark, with no data egress fees. By Renato Losio
entries.content:
Cloudflare has announced the general availability of Basin, a serverless analytics platform built on Apache Iceberg and R2 Object Storage. The managed service supports open data formats and integrates with tools such as DuckDB, Snowflake, and Apache Spark, with no data egress fees.

Introduced in preview as "Cloudflare Data Platform" just over a year ago, Basin combines data ingestion and SQL-based transformation, managed table maintenance, and distributed SQL queries, allowing developers to analyze large datasets without managing infrastructure. Marc Selwan, senior product manager at Cloudflare, and Micah Wylde, principal engineer at Cloudflare, explain why eliminating egress costs is central to the design:

A large driving force in the development and adoption of Basin is the continued growth we are seeing in the open Apache Iceberg ecosystem. (...) With Basin, you can read and write your data using any Iceberg-compatible engine, including PyIceberg, DuckDB, Snowflake, and Apache Spark. That kind of data portability is only possible with free egress, which allows developers to access their data in Cloudflare from the wide variety of tools in the ecosystem, regardless of region or cloud.

The platform combines three services: Basin Pipelines, formerly Cloudflare Pipelines, ingests events from Workers, HTTP endpoints, and Logpush, applies SQL transformations, and writes data to Apache Iceberg tables or R2; Basin Catalog manages Iceberg metadata and automates table maintenance; and Basin SQL provides a serverless, distributed SQL engine for querying Iceberg tables.

Basin aims to make analytics more accessible to smaller teams by running data ingestion, preparation, and queries on Cloudflare’s global network. This reduces the need to manage server clusters or move data between services, lowering the operational overhead of building and maintaining analytics pipelines. Selwan and Wylde explain the renaming:

Why Basin? A basin is where rivers from many sources come together to a single point. We felt that Basin perfectly captures how the platform is used: Pipelines brings data into Basin Catalog while Basin SQL makes it instantly queryable.

While some practitioners describe Basin as "open analytics infrastructure without the warehouse cathedral," Ramin Muradov, lead data analyst at PashaPay , comments:

I don't think it will knock Snowflake off its spot, at least not anytime soon. Cloudflare itself says Basin isn't a replacement for every warehouse workload. But there's a big layer of the market made up of teams whose data is too small to justify dedicated infrastructure and too big to fit in Excel. They now have an option.

Cloudflare is not the only cloud provider targeting unified analytics: as separately reported on InfoQ, AWS recently acquired DuckLabs and integrated DuckDB into Aurora PostgreSQL, aiming to simplify analytics across transactional and object storage data, while Google repositioned over the years BigQuery as the "single, unified AI-ready data platform."

Since its preview, Basin has increased ingestion capacity to 3 GB/s per stream, expanded SQL capabilities, improved Iceberg table maintenance, and added Logpush integration and Terraform support. Planned features, with no committed release dates, include real-time processing capabilities, support for the latest Iceberg specification, adaptive table-maintenance, and additional controls for data sovereignty and access management.

Cloudflare's Basin tutorial explains how to ingest events with Basin Pipelines, store them in Iceberg tables managed by Basin Catalog, and query them using Basin SQL.

entries.title: Google Finds that Technical Debt Can Derail Coding Agents Through "Agent Distraction"
entries.summary: In a recent article, Google senior staff software engineer Sam Saccone and senior staff data scientist Madhuri Garikapati highlighted the cost of agent distraction, where AI coding agents get derailed by stale technical debt, such as old TODO comments, obsolete bug references, and outdated specs, leading them to embark on unrequested "side-quests". By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
In a recent article, Google senior staff software engineer Sam Saccone and senior staff data scientist Madhuri Garikapati highlighted the cost of agent distraction, where AI coding agents get derailed by stale technical debt, such as old 

TODO
comments, obsolete bug references, and outdated specs, leading them to embark on unrequested "side-quests".

Obsolete specs, long resolved bugs, and lagging documentation no longer rest in long forgotten corners of the codebase, but rather are unintentionally ingested as context indirecting and misdirecting the next wave of coders - the agents.

According to the authors, at best, agent distraction increases token consumption and execution time; at worst, it can lead agents to "incorrect logic and decisions". To investigate this impact, they focused on 

TODO(bug/...)
comments, which, as they note, "tend to be left behind long after the underlying bug is resolved or abandoned".

By cross-referencing every TODO an agent encounters against the TODO's bug status and the user's prompt, we can automatically separate valid work from wasted detours at scale.

Using distributed traces from thousands of engineers and hundreds of millions of agent steps, Google found that approximately 13% of sessions exposed agents to inline 

TODO/FIXME
references, leading agents to take action targeting the reference bug in 6% of those cases. In most cases, the prompt did not even mention the referenced bug. Furthermore, in 41% of these unprompted detours, the agent worked on tickets that were already closed; in 57% of them they worked on bugs that were still open, but fell outside the scope of the developer's request, which the investigators classified as "scope creep".

Using a multi-way fixed-effects regression with developer-clustered standard errors, the investigators found that these detours add substantial overhead per session, with 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time.

To address this issue, Google developed scanner agents to identify and clean up obsolete TODOs across the codebase. In some cases, the agents had to inspect years of git history to be able to confirm that both the 

TODO
and the intent behind it were obsolete. However, only once confirmed this, they submitted a PR to remove the outdated reference from the codebase.

As a result of this multi-layer approach, our todo cleaner has been able to remove thousands of actually obsolete references over the last 6 months exceeding 95% acceptance from human reviewers.

The investigators conclude that tools such as presubmit analyzers, codebase scanners, and automated agents can help mitigate "agent distraction" and thus improve the effectiveness of AI coding agents.

Commenting on the finding, X user Tulasiram noted that "this is a useful reminder that comments are context too". Ryan White emphasized:

This is just junior dev behavior at machine speed. Leave a misleading comment and someone chases it for a day. Except now it happens 40 times an hour and you're paying for the tokens.

On LinkedId, user Awais Raza expressed optimism about the potential to mitigate agent distraction:

The 95%+ human acceptance of the todo cleaner is telling: it shows cleanup can be automated without losing human judgment.

Finally, Muhammad Zohaib extended this perspective, pointing out that "the same probably applies to websites: outdated pages and conflicting info make it harder for AI systems to pick the right answer."

entries.title: Pinterest and Intel Take Open-Source Profiling to Internet Scale
entries.summary: Pinterest has partnered with Intel to extend gProfiler, an open-source continuous profiler that provides production performance visibility across an internet-scale fleet of infrastructure. By Craig Risi
entries.content:
Pinterest has partnered with Intel to extend gProfiler, an open-source continuous profiler that provides production performance visibility across an internet-scale fleet of infrastructure.

Pinterest claims it operates hundreds of thousands of instances supporting 640 million monthly active users, with services written in Java, Python, C++, Go, and Node.js. At that scale, even a small efficiency improvement can have significant infrastructure and cost implications. The challenge was that engineers were using separate tools such as perf, async-profiler, and py-spy, producing fragmented profiles that were difficult to correlate across languages and machines.

Rather than building another proprietary profiling platform, Pinterest worked with Intel to extend gProfiler and contribute those capabilities back to the open-source project. The collaboration adds dynamic profiling, hardware-level telemetry, wall-time profiling, and performance-counter flame graphs, while also hardening the system for large production fleets.

gProfiler acts as an orchestration layer over several existing profilers. It combines system-wide perf data with runtime-specific tools such as async-profiler for Java and eBPF-based profiling for Python, producing a unified flame graph across the processes running on a host.

This is important for modern services where application execution crosses multiple layers. A Java application may spend time inside the JVM, native libraries, or the Linux kernel, while a Python service can involve interpreter, native, and kernel activity. Instead of requiring engineers to select and manually correlate separate profilers, gProfiler combines those views.

The agent discovers processes, starts the appropriate profilers, merges their stack traces, and uploads the resulting profile without requiring application code changes.

The new capability allows engineers to select services, hosts, or clusters and trigger profiling remotely through the UI or API. Agents normally remain dormant, consuming less than 1% CPU and 100 MB of memory, and receive profiling instructions through periodic heartbeats. You can change profiling frequency, duration, and the profilers used without redeploying the agent.

This effectively turns profiling into an operational capability rather than something that requires engineers to gain shell access to individual machines.

Integration with Intel PerfSpect allows gProfiler to collect hardware-level information such as cache behaviour, memory bandwidth, and CPU stalls. Pinterest also added PMC flame graphs, which correlate functions with hardware performance events such as cache misses and branch mispredictions.

Another addition is wall-time profiling. CPU profiling shows where processor time is being spent, but a service can still be slow while consuming relatively little CPU because threads are waiting on I/O, locks, or remote procedure calls. Wall-time profiling makes those waiting periods visible.

The gProfiler architecture separates collection from analysis. Agents run on individual hosts, while gProfiler Performance Studio aggregates and visualises the resulting profiles.

Profiles are stored in S3, passed through SQS for asynchronous indexing, and stored in ClickHouse for analytical queries. A React frontend provides flame-graph exploration, while aggregated data allows engineers to compare profiles across hosts, services, and time periods.

Pinterest and Intel also hardened the platform for production, addressing issues involving agent resource consumption, disk usage, and multi-terabyte ingestion before deploying it across the fleet.

gProfiler sits in an increasingly crowded continuous-profiling landscape. Parca and Grafana Pyroscope use eBPF and related sampling technologies to provide fleet-wide profiling, while commercial platforms such as Datadog offer continuous profiling alongside broader observability capabilities.

The distinction with gProfiler is its emphasis on system-wide, multi-runtime profiling and open-source extensibility. Rather than replacing tools such as perf or async-profiler, it orchestrates them. It also adds hardware-level profiling through Intel's tooling.

Intel's VTune provides much deeper processor and application performance analysis, but it was designed primarily as a performance-engineering tool rather than a cloud-native fleet profiler. Pinterest specifically notes that this difference influenced the decision to build on gProfiler rather than adapt VTune for its environment.

At small scale, profiling is usually something an engineer enables when a performance problem appears. At Pinterest's scale, the cost of waiting for engineers to reproduce problems or manually profile machines becomes too high. Continuous profiling provides a baseline, while dynamic profiling allows teams to investigate specific anomalies when they occur.

By combining runtime profiles, system behaviour, and hardware performance data under an open-source platform, Pinterest is effectively making profiling another layer of production observability.

entries.title: Presentation: Batch Intelligence at Scale: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience
entries.summary: Aditya Mulik explains how Walmart Global Tech deployed multi-agent LLM workflows across 4,700 stores for nightly batch inventory forecasting. He discusses tackling production hurdles - schema violations, cross-department data mismatches, and network drops - via MCP grounding and loop agents, while slashing cloud inference costs from $100k+ to $10k per month shifting from PTUs to pay-as-you-go. By
entries.content:
Transcript

Aditya Mulik: My topic today is, Batch Intelligence at Scale, which is, Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience. My name is Aditya Mulik. I work as a senior software engineer at Walmart Global Tech.

The problem I want to walk you through today is one which all retailers are wrestling with right now, which is inventory accuracy. What I want to say is the retail at massive scale, so Walmart has around 4,700 stores within the U.S. They have multiple stores in Canada, Mexico, and so on as well, but the major chunk is in the U.S. itself. There are hundreds of thousands of SKUs. There are varying departments, like varying products, any product that we can imagine of, those are all available at Walmart. The physical space is also quite large and so many items have to be tracked very carefully. The problem that each retailer is dealing with, as I mentioned about inventory accuracy, is where we have to determine what is the right inventory required for a particular occasion. If it's Thanksgiving, we have to make sure that much inventory is available at a particular point in time.

What I want to mention over here is, can we predict what inventory a department needs? I'm particularly looking for a particular department here. Can we predict what inventory a department needs for the next n number of days accurately, automatically, and at scale? Because the scale is quite large, and if you are targeting a particular department, it has to have a particular set of items available. If you are walking towards a shelf and if that shelf doesn't have a particular item available, it's not a good experience. We have to ensure that each item has to be available and in stock.

The Accuracy Imperative

The accuracy imperative. Accuracy isn't a nice-to-have, it's very mission critical, on any particular item. What we worked on was fresh food, or basically the items, you can take an example like rotisserie chicken or fresh beef, these items can expire very quickly. The store manager has to decide very accurately like, what items are there in stock and what items need to be ordered, to make sure that the inventory is very accurate for the next n number of days. The line between a stock shelf and an empty rack is what we are looking over here right now. If there are stockouts or overstock, then it could be a problem. If it's an overstock, obviously the items are going to go to waste. Either it has to be donated or it has to be thrown away. Consider this compounded across millions of square feet of retail. We have 4,700 stores, so you can imagine how critical this could be for a particular store. The next thing I'll say here is, how do we keep inventory accurate at this scale? Our first answer has to be an obvious one, we have to forecast the demand based on the history.

Backward-Looking Machine Learning Model

Now the thing is like, in Walmart, we already have machine learning models which can actually predict the amount of inventory that has to be ordered. We have backward-looking machine learning models which are trained on historical sales data to forecast future demand. We use like a year's or maybe two years of sales data, where we are trying to determine, ok, this much amount of inventory has to be ordered for the next maybe 30 days or maybe next 60 days, and so on. It's reliable for steady, recurring, and seasonal trends. Walmart is very focused on Thanksgiving. We know during Thanksgiving we have to order n number of items. That is very accurate for prediction. It's fully automated and it scales across SKUs and stores. The problem right now is sales forecasting accuracy. The pro over here is like, based on the historical trends, it can get it properly.

What if there are blind unprecedented events. Consider an example where there's a storm coming. Now the machine learning model won't be able to accurately determine if there's a storm, and if we need water or certain other items. Will that be actually available well in advance? That machine learning model might not be able to predict that. These are the things that the store manager has to deal with. They can't just rely on this particular backward trend. The question became, how do we add real-time, real-world context on top of the signals we already trust. The thing is, since we already have the machine learning models and we already know the prediction can be done in a specific way, this was an engineering challenge that came on to us, where we had to determine how should we just not rely on backward trends. Like, this is something that's going to happen, and then this number of stock has to be ordered. What if we can add some real-time context to it?

Agents, Not Monoliths: The Sequential Workflow

That's where we came up with a multi-agent — not monolith — basically a sequential workflow of agents where this agentic flow can actually determine, like get the real-time data along with some forecasting model data as well, and get the exact accurate decision that has to be given to the store manager, where these are the number of items that they need to order. How did we do that? Basically, in the sequential agentic workflow, we added multi-agent orchestration, like one agent after another, where first agent would determine, so in this case, it gathers context from various data sources for a particular department. Consider if it's a department, or like as I said about the fresh food, it's getting all the metadata from various sources like BigQuery and so on. That context is then fed to the agent, which outputs more accurate data. If it's like rotisserie chicken, it has to be ordered for the quantity that needs to be determined.

Then the second agent consumes that data, and then it synthesizes past sales data prepared by the data engineering pipeline. We have another pipeline which is set to get more context. What it does is, there's an amalgamation of two datasets which is collated, and then it is fed to another third agent data. Now this agent is quite important, which analyzes the context and output from the previous agent, and there is a grounding mechanism over here now. Consider, as I said, just a backward ML trend is not going to get us the exact prediction. There might be a weather agent, or there might be some weather API call. There could be a trending event that's happening, a sales event is happening over there. It can gather that context and it can make more accurate predictions, now that it has to order more or either less of the inventory. Then, finally, the fourth agent which produces the final natural language recommendation directive, which is like, increase the stock by this percent, and so on. That's the entire sequential workflow that we created. This was particularly targeted for a specific department.

The Output and the Human-in-the-Loop

Going to the next part, so the output, and this is the human-in-the-loop. What we were trying to do over here was, all this context generation and everything was fine, but our only goal was the store manager has to get a clear directive. The clear directive was not a dashboard, it was just a clear command. Increase apple stock 15% in produce ahead of the weekend. They are having a clear context on what they need to do. It's not just that, they are just going to increase the stock right away. There's a real-time data integration as I mentioned, which is like, MCP lets agents pull live data sources during reasoning. All of that is verified using live tools, MCPs, and so on, which is grounded properly. The critical checkpoint is, the store manager reviews each recommendation, and the store manager can either accept it or override it, because they will manually go and check and verify if there is actually a shortage of apples, if they do want to order it. There was a human in the loop in this entire pattern. This is a feature not a fallback. Human oversight in the final validation layer was catching the local context that the data cannot. That was the additional validation that the store manager was doing.

Production Rollout, and Subsequent Failures

Now this is where the important aspect comes. Then we went to production. The pilot was magic, because we tested it on maybe 10 stores or 15 stores, and then we had a clear output, coherent recommendations, and the stakeholders were quite happy about it. Then we flipped the switch to full-scale nightly runs. This was not like a real-time context where the store manager is communicating with the app, it's just a recommendation that the store manager gets during the start of the day. As Walmart stores open in the early morning, they get this recommendation and then they act upon it. Yes, we did this. We went to full chain, like all 4,700-plus stores that we rolled it out to. Then, what works at the scale of one rarely survives the scale of thousands. Here are the four failures that taught us why. Because we saw that, ok, we went to production, we made it like full chain available.

Initially for a 10-store pilot, recommendations were great, we got good feedback. There were a lot of engineering teams, data science team getting involved, and they had everything analyzed. The main thing was, me and my team's task was to get it to production, and then we started observing a lot of failures. There were four main failures which taught us what exactly happened.

I'm moving on towards the failures now. These are the common failures that we have always seen in the LLM world, and this is how we also tackled it. The very first one was hallucinations and schema violations. Here as you can see, hallucinations and schema violations were like, we had to enforce structured outputs, because the agentic workflow was getting the context, it was getting all the data, the output as well. The output was vague at times, because it was not always validated how it has to be given to the end user. Here you can see like we had to add some schema layer, which is basically to validate outputs via some JSON format of identical validation. I can give a bad example output over here. This was one of the recommendations that went to one of the store managers. As you can see over here, I think you should probably increase some stock for the weekend, maybe around 15% or so, for produce items that sell well.

It's like a coherent recommendation. It doesn't make sense, because it says that you have to increase the stock, but what stock? We don't know. Is it apples? Is it rotisserie chicken? What is it? We don't know. It's just saying that around 15%, and it should be about something that's in the produce section. Now the store manager has to go and verify which is the item that's low on stock. This didn't make sense, and it still gave a pretty high confidence. The thing is it did validate across the schema but it didn't make sense from a good output perspective. What we did is we fixed it with structured output, but also making sure that the item is also validated across a specific SKU, whether it's like which department it belongs to. If it's a produce, the item name has to be there, which is the Honeycrisp Apple right over there, and the SKU.

This confidence level made sure like this is adhering to the department that it has to be. This can be extended as possible. The stock directive, the schema which is given, and this is all validated across a common schema. As I mentioned, here's the same output. Now schema enforced, every field typed and validated: the exact SKU, item, department, and adjustment. No ambiguity left. This was the first failure.

Then, again, now the second failure. This is something that we encountered once we were full chain as well, where it was semantically wrong. What do we mean by that? You're ensuring data integrity with semantic validation. Even though we did have structured output there was a problem. The problem was the data engineering, because the workflow that was created was an overnight job, where we gathered data from various sources. Walmart has so much data for each produce, or each department. Once we pull the data, there were certain things that were getting mapped properly but certain things were not getting mapped accurately. This was a one-off situation maybe out of hundreds of items that we found out there was an issue. I can give an example over here. As you see here, everything is matching to the schema, but as we can see I have highlighted over here.
